title: Comparing a new physiotherapy treatment with usual care for people with neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome
official: Optimal physiotherapy for neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome: the IMPETUS pilot and feasibility randomised controlled trial
summary:
Background and study aims
Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome (NTOS) is a rare and disabling condition that mostly affects people of working age. It causes symptoms like pain in the neck, shoulder, arm and hand, as well as weakness and tingling in the arm, especially when doing overhead movements. While physiotherapy is the usual first-choice treatment, there are still many uncertainties about the best ways to treat NTOS. Currently, about 70% of NTOS patients don't get better with standard physiotherapy, leading to more invasive and expensive treatments like surgery. We have co-created an optimised physiotherapy treatment package for NTOS with expert clinicians and patient representatives, and we now want to test whether it is feasible and acceptable to deliver it in the NHS, and whether a larger study is needed to test its effectiveness in the future.

Who can participate?
Patients aged 18 years or over with NTOS, and physiotherapists involved in delivering their care.

What does the study involve?
We will test the new physiotherapy treatment package across NHS sites with a small group of patients and physiotherapists, to see if it's practical to use in a larger study. We will check if physiotherapists can learn to provide this new treatment, if patients are willing to use it, if the digital parts are easy to use, and if the ways we measure its effectiveness are suitable. We will involve patients with NTOS, randomly giving them either the new physiotherapy treatment package or the usual physiotherapy care they would receive. We will collect information from them using questionnaires for up to 6 months and interview a proportion of patients and therapists involved to understand how they feel about the treatment.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
There are no significant disadvantages or serious risks to taking part in this research, as both groups of patients will receive physiotherapy treatment for their NTOS. Participants may benefit from the treatment they receive, in terms of pain reduction and improved function, but we cannot promise the study will help everyone. The information gathered may help inform future research and treatment for other people with NTOS.

Where is the study run from?
University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust (UK), as part of a study sponsored by Keele University (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
December 2026 to November 2027

Who is funding the study?
The National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Mr Joel O'Sullivan, joel.o'sullivan@uhb.nhs.uk, j.o'sullivan1@keele.ac.uk

interventions.name:
Participants are randomised 1:1 to the IMPETUS physiotherapy treatment package or usual care, using mixed block randomisation stratified by site, delivered electronically via REDCap.

Both groups will receive a minimum of three face-to-face sessions over the first 3 months, lasting up to 6 months in

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Pilot & feasibility RCT:
1. Adults aged >= 18 years
2. Have a clinical diagnosis of NTOS based on the Consortium for Research and Education on Thoracic Outlet Syndrome (CORE-TOS) clinical diagnostic criteria (CDC)
3. Have physiotherapy deemed appropriate as the participants first line management
4. Be willing to participate in physiotherapy for up to 6 months (minimum three sessions)

Nested qualitative study (physiotherapist participants):
1. Treating physiotherapist involved in delivering the IMPETUS Physiotherapy treatment package to participants
2. Completed study treatments with participants and had time to reflect on their experiences
Exclusion criteria:
Pilot & feasibility RCT:
1. Recent physiotherapy for NTOS in last 3 months 
2. Previous surgery for NTOS on ipsilateral side
3. Recent history of significant trauma to affected limb
4. Co-existing arterial thoracic outlet syndrome/venous thoracic outlet syndrome (ATOS/VTOS)
5. On a surgical pathway for co-existing cervical/shoulder/peripheral nerve pathology (e.g., cervical radiculopathy/cubital or carpal tunnel syndrome)
6. Gilliatt-Sumner hand (Intrinsic atrophy)
7. No access to digital device
8. Inability to understand English language
9. Unable to partake in physiotherapy at participating site(s)

Nested qualitative study (physiotherapist participants):
1. Treating physiotherapists from usual care arm
2. Treating physiotherapists still with active patient participants
